title: A Spectroscopic Census of Cluster White Dwarfs from DESI, LAMOST, and SDSS
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ApJ
summary: Gaia has substantially expanded the sample of candidate white dwarfs (WDs) in open clusters, but many remain without spectroscopic characterization. We leverage the increasingly extensive archives of large public spectroscopic surveys to identify 62 candidate cluster WDs with available spectra from DESI, LAMOST, and SDSS. After discarding sources with very low S/N and unreliable host clusters, 44 candidates remain, including 37 non-magnetic DA WDs, of which 15 had not previously been characterized in the literature for cluster studies. We find that nine are consistent with single-star origins in their proposed host clusters, increasing the combined cluster DA initial--final mass relation (IFMR) sample to 132 WDs. All lie within $2σ$ of the best-fit IFMR from the most comprehensive recent cluster WD sample, suggesting these additions do not require recalibrating the empirical IFMR. One is a likely Hyades tidal-tail WD, providing further evidence that dynamical dispersal helps explain the long-standing WD deficit in the nearest cluster. We further compare WDs with spectra from multiple surveys. Among seven Praesepe WDs observed by both DESI and SDSS, DESI gives higher WD masses in six cases, with a mean difference of $0.067\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, while the inferred progenitor masses differ by as much as $0.459\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. More broadly, nine of ten single-star cluster DAs with DESI spectra lie above the empirical IFMR, with a mean final-mass residual of $0.06\pm0.04\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. These results show that survey-dependent differences can strongly affect cluster WD parameters, and should be considered when combining heterogeneous spectroscopy in empirical IFMR studies.

AI.tldr: Using public spectra (DESI, LAMOST, SDSS), the authors characterize 44 candidate open-cluster white dwarfs, confirm nine as likely single-star cluster members, find no need to recalibrate the empirical IFMR, and warn that survey-dependent systematics can bias cluster WD parameters.
AI.motivation: Gaia greatly expanded the sample of candidate open-cluster white dwarfs, but many lack spectroscopic characterization. This limits the size and reliability of the cluster-white-dwarf initial-final mass relation (IFMR) sample, which is crucial for constraining stellar evolution and for testing cluster membership questions such as the white-dwarf deficit in the Hyades.
AI.method: The authors cross-matched candidate cluster white dwarfs with large public spectroscopic archives (DESI, LAMOST, SDSS), identifying 62 candidates with available spectra. After rejecting very low S/N sources and unreliable host clusters, 44 candidates remained, including 37 non-magnetic DA white dwarfs (15 previously uncharacterized for cluster studies). They analyzed spectra to derive white-dwarf and progenitor masses, assessed single-star cluster consistency, and compared parameters for white dwarfs observed by multiple surveys (e.g., seven Praesepe WDs in both DESI and SDSS).
AI.result: Nine of the 44 candidates are consistent with single-star origins in their proposed host clusters, increasing the combined cluster DA IFMR sample to 132 white dwarfs. All lie within 2σ of the best-fit IFMR from the most comprehensive recent cluster WD sample, so no recalibration is required. One is a likely Hyades tidal-tail white dwarf, supporting dynamical dispersal as an explanation for the Hyades WD deficit. For the seven Praesepe WDs observed by both DESI and SDSS, DESI yields higher masses in six cases, with a mean difference of 0.067 M_sun and progenitor-mass differences up to 0.459 M_sun. Nine of ten single-star cluster DAs with DESI spectra lie above the empirical IFMR, with a mean final-mass residual of 0.06 ± 0.04 M_sun.
AI.conclusion: Archival public spectroscopy can efficiently characterize candidate cluster white dwarfs and modestly expand the empirical cluster IFMR sample without requiring recalibration. However, survey-dependent differences (e.g., DESI vs. SDSS) can strongly affect inferred white-dwarf and progenitor parameters, so heterogeneous spectroscopy must be treated carefully when combining data in empirical IFMR studies.

title: What does self-supervision add to engineered features for stellar light curves?
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://github.com/BrightonLiu-zZ/stellar-ssl/tree/arxiv-v1
summary: TESS light curves encode a star's pulsation, rotation, binarity and oscillations, among other physical properties, but the survey produces far more light curves than can be labelled by hand. Astronomers have engineered a few dozen physically motivated features from them, which together remain a strong baseline. Previous work has trained encoders on light curves and judged them by their own downstream scores, but has not asked what they add to the engineered features. We pre-train a convolutional encoder on unlabelled TESS light curves to predict each window's latent representation from those of its neighbours. We then freeze it, add its features to the 25 engineered features, and read the combination out with one fixed linear probe on ten tasks: five variability classes, four asteroseismic targets and rotation period. Adding the learned features improves the readout on 7 of 10 tasks over the engineered features alone, where an untrained encoder does not. The combination also outperforms two networks trained end-to-end on the same labelled stars on most tasks. An encoder trained without labels therefore gives astronomers new features that complement the ones they already use rather than replace them.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised convolutional encoder is pre-trained on unlabelled TESS light curves by predicting each window's latent representation from its neighbours; frozen features added to 25 engineered features improve a fixed linear probe on 7 of 10 tasks.
AI.motivation: TESS produces far more light curves than can be labelled by hand. Astronomers rely on a few dozen physically motivated engineered features that remain a strong baseline, and prior encoder work only reported its own downstream scores without testing what it adds to those engineered features.
AI.method: Pre-train a convolutional encoder on unlabelled TESS light curves with a neighbour-prediction objective (predict each window's latent representation from its neighbours' representations). Freeze the encoder, concatenate its features with the 25 engineered features, and evaluate with one fixed linear probe across ten tasks: five variability classes, four asteroseismic targets, and rotation period. Compare against engineered features alone, an untrained encoder, and two end-to-end trained networks.
AI.result: Adding the learned features improves the readout on 7 of 10 tasks relative to engineered features alone, whereas an untrained encoder does not. The combination also outperforms two end-to-end networks trained on the same labelled stars on most tasks.
AI.conclusion: An encoder trained without labels yields new features that complement, rather than replace, astronomers' existing engineered features.

title: Mapping Wolf-Rayet winds with spectro-interferometry I. Detection of multiple co-rotating interaction regions in WR 6
comment: 14 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to A&A, comments welcome
summary: WR 6 is the prototype for periodic variability due to large-scale wind structures in Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars, showing a consistent periodicity of 3.76 d in photometry, spectroscopy, and polarimetry. However, the origin of this variability is debated, attributed either to corotating interaction regions (CIRs) or a low-mass companion. We use time-resolved interferometry to investigate the origin of periodic variability in WR 6. We aim to detect and characterize structures in the stellar winds of WR 6 and discriminate between the CIR and low-mass companion scenarios. Using the extended configuration of the Auxiliary Telescopes at VLTI, we obtained six GRAVITY epochs over six months to search for the presence and variability of wind-structures in WR 6. We also obtained complementary spectroscopic observations during one of the epochs to monitor contemporaneous spectral line variability. For all six epochs of GRAVITY observations: (i) WR 6 is consistent with a single star and has no spatially resolved companion detected above $M\gtrsim6\,M_\odot$; (ii) The He I line-emitting region is spatially resolved, while the He II lines remain unresolved, consistent with atmosphere models; (iii) Around 2.19 $μ$m, discrete line-emitting features offset from the center of the star are detected. The number, positions, and wavelengths of these features vary across epochs. Spectroscopic monitoring reveals spectral line residuals that broadly correspond to the two features seen in the GRAVITY data of the fifth epoch. Finally, the first three epochs, observed on three consecutive nights, show significant variability in these features but cannot be directly linked across epochs. We thus report the detection of multiple large-scale structures in the wind of WR 6 with VLTI/GRAVITY. We favor CIRs as their likely origin owing to temporal and spatial variability that cannot be reconciled with a low-mass companion.

AI.tldr: VLTI/GRAVITY interferometry of WR 6 resolves multiple discrete wind-emission features offset from the star that vary across epochs, with no companion above ~6 M_sun; the authors favor corotating interaction regions over a low-mass companion as the origin of the 3.76 d periodicity.
AI.motivation: WR 6 is the prototype for periodic (3.76 d) variability in Wolf-Rayet stars, observed consistently in photometry, spectroscopy, and polarimetry, yet its origin is debated: either large-scale wind structures (corotating interaction regions, CIRs) or a low-mass companion. Existing data lack the spatial resolution needed to distinguish these scenarios.
AI.method: Time-resolved interferometry with the extended configuration of the VLTI Auxiliary Telescopes: six GRAVITY epochs over six months searching for wind structures and their variability. Complementary spectroscopic observations during one epoch monitored contemporaneous spectral line variability.
AI.result: Across all six GRAVITY epochs: (i) WR 6 is consistent with a single star, with no spatially resolved companion above M ≳ 6 M_sun; (ii) the He I line-emitting region is spatially resolved while He II lines remain unresolved, consistent with atmosphere models; (iii) near 2.19 μm, discrete line-emitting features offset from the stellar center are detected, whose number, positions, and wavelengths vary across epochs. Spectroscopic monitoring reveals line residuals broadly matching the two features seen in GRAVITY data of the fifth epoch. The first three epochs, on three consecutive nights, show significant variability in these features but cannot be directly linked across epochs.
AI.conclusion: Multiple large-scale structures are detected in the wind of WR 6 with VLTI/GRAVITY. Their temporal and spatial variability cannot be reconciled with a low-mass companion, so CIRs are favored as the likely origin of the periodic variability.

title: TESS Pulsation Timing Reveals the JWST Calibration Star HD 158485 as a Double-pulsator Binary
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: HD~158485 is an A-type $δ$~Scuti star in the CALSPEC network and the JWST absolute-flux calibration program. Gaia DR3 assigns it a binary classification probability close to unity but provides no orbital solution. Using TESS observations from Sectors 14--26, 40--41, 47--60, and 73--86, we measure the pulsation phases of six $δ$~Scuti modes. The frequencies form two groups with opposite light-travel-time delays, revealing two pulsating components. A direct light-curve forward model yields an orbital period of $P_{\rm orb}=382.80^{+0.80}_{-0.76}$~d, eccentricity $e=0.242^{+0.045}_{-0.046}$, projected light-time amplitudes of $195.8^{+9.2}_{-8.9}$ and $239.7^{+6.8}_{-6.8}$~s, and a dynamical mass ratio of $q=M_B/M_A=0.818^{+0.046}_{-0.045}$. A blind prediction based only on the first two long TESS campaigns reproduces the third campaign without updating the orbital parameters, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of $r=0.983$. Its held-out rms is 83.8~s, compared with 289.9~s when the period is fixed at 365.25~d. A 5.15-$σ$ Hipparcos--Gaia EDR3 proper-motion anomaly independently indicates unresolved astrometric motion. The unresolved companion can also affect spectrophotometric predictions: a conditional PB2-constrained two-atmosphere model differs from the corresponding single-star atmosphere prediction by 1.6\% over 1--5~$μ$m and 2.5\% over 5--28~$μ$m. HD~158485 therefore shows that a calibration-relevant binary can lack a catalogued orbital solution while two independent pulsation clocks reveal and measure its orbit.

AI.tldr: HD~158485 is a pulsating binary δ~Scuti star used for JWST flux calibration; its orbit, previously absent from Gaia, is revealed and measured through pulsation phase timing, and the unresolved companion is shown to bias spectrophotometric predictions at the percent level.
AI.motivation: HD~158485 is a CALSPEC standard and JWST absolute-flux calibrator, so any unresolved companion can contaminate calibration. Gaia DR3 flags it as a binary with near-unity probability yet supplies no orbital solution, leaving the companion's effect unquantified. The paper aims to detect and characterize this hidden orbit and assess its impact on spectrophotometric predictions.
AI.method: Using TESS photometry from Sectors 14–26, 40–41, 47–60, and 73–86, the authors measure pulsation phases of six δ~Scuti modes. The mode frequencies split into two groups with opposite light-travel-time delays, indicating two pulsating components. A direct light-curve forward model fits the orbital parameters (period, eccentricity, projected light-time amplitudes, mass ratio). A blind prediction test uses only the first two long TESS campaigns to predict the third without updating parameters. A 5.15-σ Hipparcos–Gaia EDR3 proper-motion anomaly is used as an independent astrometric check, and a PB2-constrained two-atmosphere model quantifies the companion's spectrophotometric effect.
AI.result: The forward model yields P_orb=382.80 (+0.80/−0.76) d, e=0.242 (+0.045/−0.046), projected light-time amplitudes 195.8 (+9.2/−8.9) s and 239.7 (+6.8/−6.8) s, and q=M_B/M_A=0.818 (+0.046/−0.045). Blind prediction from the first two campaigns reproduces the third with Pearson r=0.983 and held-out rms 83.8 s, versus 289.9 s when the period is fixed at 365.25 d. A 5.15-σ Hipparcos–Gaia EDR3 proper-motion anomaly independently confirms unresolved astrometric motion. The two-atmosphere model differs from the single-star prediction by 1.6% over 1–5 μm and 2.5% over 5–28 μm.
AI.conclusion: HD~158485 demonstrates that a calibration-relevant binary can lack a catalogued orbital solution while two independent pulsation clocks reveal and measure its orbit. The unresolved companion introduces percent-level biases in spectrophotometric predictions, so pulsation-timing provides both an orbital solution and a warning for absolute-flux calibration.

title: The $R$-Process Alliance: On J0010$-$1735, an Accreted, Chemically Unusual, Metal-poor Star with $R$-process Enhancement
summary: We present a detailed chemo-dynamical analysis of the chemically peculiar very metal-poor ([Fe/H]$=-2.22\pm 0.11$) Milky Way (MW) halo star, 2MASS J00101758$-$1735387 (hereafter J0010-1735), discovered by the $R$-Process Alliance. We derive abundances for 45 elements, including 28 neutron-capture elements, and confirm that \thestar\ is highly $r$-process-enhanced, with [Eu/Fe]=$+1.30$. The light, $α$, and Fe-peak element abundances ratios relative to Fe are all sub-solar, aside from C, Si, and most extremely, Ca. We investigate three possible formation scenarios based on the star's chemical abundances and orbital kinematics: whether it formed in the \textit{in-situ} MW halo, in a MW dwarf galaxy satellite, or in a satellite of the Magellanic Cloud system. Using the position of \thestar\ in the [Mg/Mn]--[Al/Fe] plane, the abundance pattern of both the light and heavy elements, and the kinematics, we conclude that J0010-1735 most plausibly originated in a now-disrupted ultra-faint dwarf galaxy that was accreted into the MW halo. We examine potential chemical enrichment scenarios of J0010-1735, including one similar to the $r$-process-enhanced UFD Reticulum II, or enrichment via a sub-Chandrasekhar Type Ia SNe, potentially supplemented by a Ca-rich gap transient and by a separate neutron-rich site that facilitated $r$-process enrichment. A nuclear cosmochronometric age of $12.5\pm4.2$ Gyr is derived from the [Th/Eu] ratio, consistent with an ancient origin in one of the earliest star-forming systems in the universe.

AI.tldr: A detailed chemo-dynamical study of the highly r-process-enhanced, very metal-poor halo star J0010-1735 reveals its abundance pattern (45 elements, 28 neutron-capture) and orbital kinematics, indicating it most likely originated in a disrupted ultra-faint dwarf galaxy accreted into the Milky Way halo, with a cosmochronometric age of 12.5 ± 4.2 Gyr.
AI.motivation: The origin of chemically peculiar, very metal-poor, r-process-enhanced halo stars is debated. Distinguishing whether such stars formed in situ in the Milky Way halo, in a Milky Way dwarf galaxy satellite, or in a satellite of the Magellanic Cloud system is key to understanding early galactic chemical enrichment and accretion history. J0010-1735 provides a test case for these formation channels.
AI.method: The authors performed a chemo-dynamical analysis of J0010-1735 ([Fe/H] = -2.22 ± 0.11), deriving abundances for 45 elements including 28 neutron-capture elements. They assessed three formation scenarios using the star's chemical abundance ratios and orbital kinematics. Diagnostic tools included the [Mg/Mn]-[Al/Fe] plane, light- and heavy-element abundance patterns, and kinematics. They also examined enrichment scenarios, including comparison to the r-process-enhanced UFD Reticulum II and enrichment via sub-Chandrasekhar Type Ia SNe, possibly supplemented by a Ca-rich gap transient and a separate neutron-rich r-process site, and derived a nuclear cosmochronometric age from the [Th/Eu] ratio.
AI.result: J0010-1735 is confirmed as highly r-process-enhanced ([Eu/Fe] = +1.30). Light, α, and Fe-peak abundance ratios relative to Fe are sub-solar, except for C, Si, and most notably Ca. Based on the [Mg/Mn]-[Al/Fe] plane, abundance patterns, and kinematics, the star most plausibly originated in a now-disrupted ultra-faint dwarf galaxy accreted into the Milky Way halo. A nuclear cosmochronometric age of 12.5 ± 4.2 Gyr was derived from the [Th/Eu] ratio.
AI.conclusion: J0010-1735 most likely formed in a disrupted ultra-faint dwarf galaxy accreted into the Milky Way halo, consistent with an ancient origin in one of the earliest star-forming systems in the universe. Its enrichment may resemble r-process-enhanced UFD Reticulum II or proceed via sub-Chandrasekhar Type Ia SNe potentially supplemented by a Ca-rich gap transient and a separate neutron-rich r-process site.

title: Radial increase of the compensated interplanetary magnetic field magnitude as a result of the growth of spherically polarized Alfvén waves
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures
summary: Measurements from the NASA Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission demonstrate that inside $\sim20$ solar radii ($\Rs$) the magnitude of the interplanetary magnetic field does not fall off simply as $1/R^2$, with $\avg{|B|}\,R^2$ 15--20\% below its value at $\sim60\,\Rs$. Here we use PSP magnetic field measurements over $10.6$--$56.8\,\Rs$ to show that the outward rise of $\avg{|B|}\,R^2$ is not due to the global structure of the heliospheric magnetic field or proximity to the heliospheric current sheet but is the direct result of the growth of large-amplitude, spherically polarized Alfvén waves (so-called `switchbacks'). Over the same distance range, $\avg{B_R}\,R^2$ stays constant, so that the sector-signed radial flux is conserved. The wave amplitude $ε= B_{\perp,{\rm rms}}/\avg{B_\parallel}$ grows from $0.26$ to $0.57$ as $R^{1/2}\cosα$, and $\avg{|B|}/\avg{B_R}$ rises by $20\%$. A simple model parametrized by the broadening of the distribution of deflection angles reproduces the effect to high accuracy. These results demonstrate that as the relative wave amplitudes grow with increasing solar distance, a dynamo-like process operates to enhance the field magnitude by up to $20\%$. By enhancing magnetic pressure this has implications for the large scale solar wind structure in the low-beta inner heliosphere, as well as partially resolving the long-standing discrepancy between remote measurements of the solar magnetic field and those made in situ by earlier missions farther from the Sun.

AI.tldr: PSP measurements reveal that the non-1/R² radial falloff of interplanetary magnetic field magnitude inside ~20 Rs is caused by growing, spherically polarized Alfvén waves (switchbacks), not by global heliospheric structure.
AI.motivation: Parker Solar Probe observed that inside ~20 solar radii the magnetic field magnitude does not fall off as 1/R², with ⟨|B|⟩R² being 15–20% below its value at ~60 Rs. The origin of this anomalous deficit needed explanation, as it affects solar wind structure and the long-standing discrepancy between remote and in situ magnetic field measurements.
AI.method: Analysis of PSP magnetic field measurements over 10.6–56.8 solar radii; comparing ⟨|B|⟩R², ⟨B_R⟩R², wave amplitude ε = B_⊥,rms/⟨B_∥⟩, and ⟨|B|⟩/⟨B_R⟩; constructing a model parametrized by the broadening of the deflection angle distribution.
AI.result: The outward rise of ⟨|B|⟩R² is due to growth of large-amplitude spherically polarized Alfvén waves (switchbacks), not global field structure or proximity to the heliospheric current sheet. ⟨B_R⟩R² remains constant (conserved sector-signed radial flux). Wave amplitude ε grows from 0.26 to 0.57 as R^{1/2} cosα, and ⟨|B|⟩/⟨B_R⟩ rises by 20%. The deflection-angle-broadening model reproduces the effect to high accuracy.
AI.conclusion: As relative wave amplitudes grow with increasing solar distance, a dynamo-like process enhances the field magnitude by up to 20%. This raises magnetic pressure, affecting large-scale solar wind structure in the low-beta inner heliosphere and partially resolving the discrepancy between remote and in situ magnetic field measurements.

title: Assessing the impact of background subtraction on a dust-free corona
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Context. White-light observations of the solar corona contain contributions from both the electron-scattered K-corona and the dust-scattered F-corona. Because the diffuse F-corona dominates the measured intensity at altitudes of approximately 4 $R_{\odot}$ and above, background subtraction techniques are routinely employed to isolate the electron corona in coronagraph observations. Aims. Since no direct observational "ground truth" for the K-corona exists, the amount of coronal signal that is inadvertently removed by background subtraction methods remains unknown. We aim to quantify, for the first time, the impact of background subtraction on the inferred large-scale structure and brightness of the solar corona. Methods. We use a 32-day simulation based on a novel near-real-time, data-assimilative, time-evolving magnetohydrodynamic model to generate synthetic white-light observables. Because these synthetic observations are free from dust and instrumental stray-light contributions, they provide direct access to the "true" K-corona and enable a quantitative assessment of the effects of background subtraction. Results. We find that background subtraction generally preserves the large-scale morphology of the electron corona, including the locations and shapes of major coronal structures. However, the procedure systematically modifies the relative brightness of different features and removes a non-negligible fraction of the K-coronal signal. Conclusions. Although standard background subtraction techniques successfully recover the overall appearance of the electron corona, they can alter its quantitative photometric properties. These findings should be considered when interpreting coronal brightness measurements and deriving physical properties from processed white-light observations.

AI.tldr: Using a 32-day data-assimilative MHD simulation to generate dust-free synthetic white-light observations, this study provides the first quantitative assessment of how background subtraction affects the inferred K-corona, finding that it preserves large-scale morphology but systematically biases relative brightness and removes a non-negligible fraction of the K-coronal signal.
AI.motivation: White-light coronal observations mix the electron-scattered K-corona with the dust-scattered F-corona, and because the diffuse F-corona dominates beyond roughly 4 solar radii, background subtraction is routinely used to isolate the electron corona. Yet no direct observational ground truth for the K-corona exists, so the amount of coronal signal inadvertently removed by these methods has remained unknown, and its impact on inferred large-scale structure and brightness had never been quantified.
AI.method: A 32-day simulation based on a near-real-time, data-assimilative, time-evolving magnetohydrodynamic model was used to generate synthetic white-light observables. Being free of dust and instrumental stray-light contributions, these synthetic observations give direct access to the "true" K-corona and allow quantitative evaluation of background subtraction effects.
AI.result: Background subtraction generally preserves the large-scale morphology of the electron corona, including the locations and shapes of major coronal structures. However, it systematically modifies the relative brightness of different features and removes a non-negligible fraction of the K-coronal signal.
AI.conclusion: Standard background subtraction techniques successfully recover the overall appearance of the electron corona but can alter its quantitative photometric properties. These effects should be taken into account when interpreting coronal brightness measurements and deriving physical properties from processed white-light observations.

title: An asteroseismic age estimate for the Pleiades using a neural-network emulator of rotating $δ$ Scuti pulsation models
comment: 26 pages, 21 figures, 14 tables
summary: Asteroseismology of $δ$ Sct stars has strong potential for determining the ages of young stars through individual mode fitting. We present a neural-network emulator trained on approximately 46 million rotating pulsation models. From stellar mass, metallicity, age, and equatorial rotation velocity, it predicts 12 classical observables, two asteroseismic scalars, and the p mode, f mode and low-order g mode frequencies for degrees $\ell=0$-3, including the individual $m$ components of rotationally split multiplets. We couple the emulator to nested sampling through a multivariate likelihood that propagates correlated emulator residuals, making full Bayesian posterior exploration practical. Applied to five $δ$ Sct stars in the Pleiades observed by TESS, the framework gives mutually consistent individual asteroseismic ages of 107-117 Myr. Combining their age posteriors gives a cluster age of $113.3\pm4.5$ Myr (statistical), consistent with the $112 \pm 5$ Myr lithium-depletion-boundary age and the 110-160 Myr range from rotating-isochrone fitting. Together with spectroscopic $v\sin i$, the inferred equatorial velocities also provide post-fit inclination estimates. Separate perturbed-grid tests using 100 matched synthetic pairs per input-physics variation give median absolute age shifts of $2.1$, $2.3$, and $5.2$ Myr for $|Δf_{\rm ov}|=0.005$, $|Δα_{\rm MLT}|=0.1$, and $|ΔY|=0.02$, respectively; the corresponding 90th percentile shifts are $6.5$, $7.6$, and $16.2$ Myr. These tests describe conditional population sensitivities, not a systematic uncertainty on the Pleiades age. Together, the cluster-age agreement and the scale of these input-physics sensitivities support $δ$ Sct asteroseismology as a complementary age estimation method for young stars.

AI.tldr: A neural-network emulator trained on ~46 million rotating δ Sct pulsation models enables full Bayesian asteroseismic age fitting, yielding mutually consistent individual ages of 107–117 Myr for five Pleiades δ Sct stars and a combined cluster age of 113.3 ± 4.5 Myr.
AI.motivation: δ Sct asteroseismology has strong potential for dating young stars via individual mode fitting, but the computational expense of rotating pulsation models and correlated model residuals makes full Bayesian posterior exploration impractical.
AI.method: A neural-network emulator trained on ~46 million rotating pulsation models predicts, from mass, metallicity, age, and equatorial rotation velocity, 12 classical observables, two asteroseismic scalars, and p/f/low-order g mode frequencies for ℓ=0–3 including individual m components of rotationally split multiplets. It is coupled to nested sampling via a multivariate likelihood propagating correlated emulator residuals.
AI.result: Applied to five Pleiades δ Sct stars observed by TESS, individual asteroseismic ages are mutually consistent at 107–117 Myr; combined cluster age is 113.3 ± 4.5 Myr, consistent with the 112 ± 5 Myr lithium-depletion-boundary age and 110–160 Myr rotating-isochrone range. Spectroscopic v sin i plus inferred equatorial velocities give post-fit inclination estimates. Perturbed-grid tests (100 matched synthetic pairs per variation) give median absolute age shifts of 2.1, 2.3, and 5.2 Myr for |Δf_ov|=0.005, |Δα_MLT|=0.1, and |ΔY|=0.02, with 90th percentile shifts of 6.5, 7.6, and 16.2 Myr.
AI.conclusion: The cluster-age agreement and the magnitude of input-physics sensitivities support δ Sct asteroseismology as a complementary age estimation method for young stars, with the perturbed-grid tests describing conditional population sensitivities rather than a systematic uncertainty on the Pleiades age.

title: Integration of a CME Flux Rope Model with Magnetic Field Draping in Heliospheric Simulations
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Accurate prediction of the magnetic structure of interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs) remains a key challenge in space weather forecasting. Despite several efforts using global MHD modeling, it remains difficult to deduce a flux-rope solution that can accurately and reliably reproduce the magnetic structure of a CME. We present FROST (Flux Rope embedded in the Solar Magnetic Field), a new flux-rope model implementation within the European Heliospheric Forecast Information Asset (EUHFORIA), featuring an initially force-free toroidal flux rope embedded in the low-coronal magnetic field. FROST employs a novel embedding technique that self-consistently generates a draping magnetic field around the flux-rope, ensuring continuity of the normal magnetic field component at the CME boundary. The dynamics of the flux-rope in the low and middle corona is solved by a non-uniform advection constrained by the observed kinematics of the event. This results in a global, non-toroidal, stretched loop-like magnetic structure. At heliospheric distances, the evolution is modeled as an MHD process using EUHFORIA. We validate the FROST model implementation by simulating the CME event of 2013 April 11 and comparing the results with in situ magnetic field measurements at 1 au. The modeled magnetic field profiles of the flux-rope exhibit strong agreement with the observations, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.64-0.93 for Bx, 0.92-0.95 for By, and 0.82-0.87 for Bz component of the magnetic field. These results demonstrate the capability of the proposed flux-rope model to significantly improve ICME magnetic field prediction, highlighting its strong potential for advancing space-weather forecasting capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FROST, a new flux-rope model within EUHFORIA that embeds a force-free toroidal flux rope in the low-coronal magnetic field using a self-consistent draping technique, and validates it against the 2013 April 11 CME event, achieving strong agreement with in situ magnetic field measurements at 1 au.
AI.motivation: Accurately predicting the magnetic structure of interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs) is a major challenge in space weather forecasting. Existing global MHD modeling efforts struggle to derive a flux-rope solution that reliably reproduces CME magnetic structure.
AI.method: FROST (Flux Rope embedded in the Solar Magnetic Field) is a flux-rope model implementation within EUHFORIA. It features an initially force-free toroidal flux rope embedded in the low-coronal magnetic field via a novel embedding technique that self-consistently generates a draping magnetic field around the flux rope, maintaining continuity of the normal magnetic field component at the CME boundary. Low- and middle-coronal dynamics are solved by non-uniform advection constrained by observed event kinematics, producing a global, non-toroidal, stretched loop-like magnetic structure. Heliospheric evolution is modeled as an MHD process using EUHFORIA.
AI.result: Validation against the 2013 April 11 CME event shows modeled flux-rope magnetic field profiles agree strongly with in situ measurements at 1 au, with correlation coefficients of 0.64-0.93 for Bx, 0.92-0.95 for By, and 0.82-0.87 for Bz.
AI.conclusion: FROST significantly improves ICME magnetic field prediction and shows strong potential for advancing space-weather forecasting capabilities.

title: Grand minima and intermittency in near-critical convection-driven dynamos
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, submitted to Astron. Astrophys
summary: Context: Solar magnetism exhibits long-term variations on timescales of decades to centuries. Aims: The main aim is to study how the supercriticality of the dynamo affects the variability of magnetic fields on timescales relevant to the Sun. Methods: Three-dimensional rotating magnetohydrodynamic simulations in a spherical wedge geometry are used to produce self-consistent convection-driven dynamos. The supercriticality of the dynamo is controlled by varying the magnetic diffusivity. Results: The main result is that long-term variability of the dynamo increases with decreasing supercriticality of the dynamo and that cases nearest to the onset of dynamo action show extended grand minima-like periods of low activity. The simulations fall in three classes where the least supercritical cases show the largest variations of magnetic activity and where the flow including differential rotation is almost unaffected by the magnetic field. In the cases with the highest supercriticality the magnetic field is permanently strong and differential rotation permanently quenched, both having relatively little temporal variation. In an intermediate regime both the magnetic fields and differential rotation exhibit strong anticorrelated fluctuations. Conclusions: The occurrence of grand minima in the Sun has been conjectured to be due to a weakly supercritical dynamo. The current results support this idea and suggest that the absence of grand minima in earlier global dynamo simulations is because their large-scale dynamos were too supercritical. Furthermore, the current results suggest that the effect of the magnetic field on differential rotation is negligible if the average rms-field is less than about 2~kG.

AI.tldr: Supercriticality of a convection-driven dynamo controls long-term magnetic variability: less supercritical dynamos show larger variations and grand minima-like periods.
AI.motivation: Solar magnetism varies on decadal-to-centennial timescales and exhibits grand minima-like episodes; the study aims to determine how dynamo supercriticality governs magnetic field variability on solar-relevant timescales.
AI.method: 3D rotating magnetohydrodynamic simulations in a spherical wedge geometry generate self-consistent convection-driven dynamos, with supercriticality controlled by varying the magnetic diffusivity.
AI.result: Long-term variability increases with decreasing supercriticality. Three regimes emerge: (1) least supercritical cases have largest activity variations and nearly unaffected differential rotation; (2) highest supercriticality cases have permanently strong fields, permanently quenched differential rotation, and little temporal variation; (3) intermediate cases show strong anticorrelated fluctuations of magnetic field and differential rotation.
AI.conclusion: Grand minima may arise from a weakly supercritical dynamo; their absence in earlier global dynamo simulations likely stems from overly supercritical large-scale dynamos. The magnetic field's effect on differential rotation is negligible when the average rms field is below about 2 kG.

title: From the QBO to Rieger-type periods: Explaining extreme solar events by tidally triggered magneto-Rossby waves
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures
summary: It has recently been demonstrated that the occurrence of extreme solar events is governed by a phase-stable period close to 1.723 years (629.29 days). According to our previously developed tidally-synchronized solar dynamo model, this is one of the periods resulting from two-planet spring tides exerted by the tidally dominant planets Venus, Earth and Jupiter, which trigger magneto-Rossby waves in the solar tachocline. Overall, the squared sum of these three waves incorporates nine periods ranging from 59 to 629 days. Using a standard Rayleigh test, we demonstrate that all nine of these periods can be identified in the data on extreme solar events. For the latter, we use a combination of 72 ground-level enhancement (GLE) events with various X-flare data, the number of which increases when the threshold is successively lowered from X10 to X1. To identify the spectral peaks, it is necessary to analyze the sidebands that emerge due to the modulation with the longer-term periods such as the 11-year Schwabe cycle and the third harmonics of the Hale cycle. In this framework, the seminal Rieger period of 154 days is re-interpreted as the lower sideband of 146 days which is the quarter of the synodic period of Venus and Earth.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that all nine periods (59–629 days) predicted by a tidally-synchronized solar dynamo model—arising from Venus, Earth, and Jupiter spring tides—can be identified in extreme solar event data via a Rayleigh test, with the famous Rieger period reinterpreted as a sideband.
AI.motivation: Extreme solar events appear governed by a phase-stable ~1.723-year (629.29-day) period, and the authors' previously developed tidally-synchronized solar dynamo model attributes such periods to planetary tidal forcing. This study aims to test whether the full set of predicted periodicities is actually present in solar event records.
AI.method: The squared sum of three tidally-triggered magneto-Rossby waves (from Venus, Earth, Jupiter) yields nine periods from 59 to 629 days. The authors apply a standard Rayleigh test to extreme solar event data—72 ground-level enhancement (GLE) events combined with X-flare data whose counts rise as the threshold is lowered from X10 to X1. Sidebands from modulation with longer-term periods (the 11-year Schwabe cycle and the third harmonic of the Hale cycle) are analyzed to resolve the spectral peaks.
AI.result: All nine predicted periods are identified in the extreme solar event data. The classic Rieger period of 154 days is reinterpreted as the lower sideband of a 146-day period, which is one quarter of the Venus–Earth synodic period.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the tidally-synchronized solar dynamo model, demonstrating that planetary tidal forcing imprints a coherent set of periodicities on extreme solar events, and reframe the Rieger period within a planetary-tidal framework.

title: SiO Maser Line-width Diagnostics of AGB Stars and Red Supergiants: The RSG-adjacent Region in the FWZI--Luminosity Plane
summary: We investigate whether SiO maser line profiles can distinguish asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars from red supergiants (RSGs) and identify unusual AGB-classified sources near the RSG regime. We compiled 2,956 detected SiO maser spectra for 1,551 objects and constructed reference samples of 1,068 O-rich AGB stars and 36 RSGs. The full width at zero intensity (FWZI) was reliably measured for 1,020 AGB stars and 32 RSGs. AGB stars are concentrated at narrow line widths: 81.5% have FWZI <10 km s^-1, whereas 81.2% of RSGs have FWZI >15 km s^-1 and none has FWZI <10 km s^-1. Infrared two-color diagrams provide only partial separation. Combining FWZI with luminosities based primarily on quality-filtered Gaia/Bailer-Jones distances, with independent literature distances for several RSGs, reveals a weak tendency for wider SiO maser lines at higher luminosities but no clean boundary. We therefore define an empirical RSG-adjacent region in the FWZI-luminosity plane, 15 <= FWZI <= 26.6 km s^-1 and 3.9 <= log(L/L_sun) <= 4.9, to characterize the high-luminosity, broad-line tail of the AGB-classified sample. Ten sources fall within this region. Using infrared SEDs, DUSTY fits, OH/H2O maser information, and variability, we find that six are most naturally interpreted as luminous AGB-like objects, two warrant follow-up to assess possible high-initial-mass AGB, RSG-like, or SAGB-related interpretations, and two are less securely constrained because of poor DUSTY fits. The RSG-adjacent region is therefore a physically mixed screening space, not a definitive classification box, for selecting high-priority follow-up targets.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether SiO maser line profiles (specifically FWZI) can separate O-rich AGB stars from RSGs, and defines an empirical "RSG-adjacent" region in the FWZI–luminosity plane to flag unusually broad-lined, high-luminosity AGB-classified sources for follow-up.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing O-rich AGB stars from RSGs is often difficult because their observational properties overlap, particularly near the high-luminosity boundary. A simple, widely available diagnostic that could help separate the two classes and reveal misclassified or physically unusual sources would be valuable, motivating an assessment of SiO maser line widths as such a discriminator.
AI.method: Compiled 2,956 detected SiO maser spectra for 1,551 objects, building reference samples of 1,068 O-rich AGB stars and 36 RSGs with reliably measured full width at zero intensity (FWZI; 1,020 AGB stars, 32 RSGs). Compared FWZI distributions and infrared two-color diagrams, then combined FWZI with luminosities derived mainly from quality-filtered Gaia/Bailer-Jones distances (with literature distances for several RSGs) to define an empirical RSG-adjacent region in the FWZI–luminosity plane. Characterized the ten sources inside this region using infrared SEDs, DUSTY fits, OH/H2O maser information, and variability.
AI.result: AGB stars are concentrated at narrow line widths (81.5% with FWZI <10 km s^-1), while 81.2% of RSGs have FWZI >15 km s^-1 and none has FWZI <10 km s^-1. Infrared two-color diagrams provide only partial separation. The FWZI–luminosity plane shows a weak trend toward wider lines at higher luminosities but no clean boundary. The empirical RSG-adjacent region is defined as 15 <= FWZI <= 26.6 km s^-1 and 3.9 <= log(L/L_sun) <= 4.9. Of the ten sources within it, six are best interpreted as luminous AGB-like objects, two warrant follow-up (possible high-initial-mass AGB, RSG-like, or SAGB-related), and two remain poorly constrained due to poor DUSTY fits.
AI.conclusion: SiO maser FWZI is an effective statistical discriminator between O-rich AGB stars and RSGs, but it is not a definitive classifier. The RSG-adjacent region in the FWZI–luminosity plane is a physically mixed screening space rather than a classification box, useful for selecting high-priority follow-up targets rather than assigning final classifications.

title: Aditya-L1 and SDO Observations of a Confined X-Class Flare with an EUV Late Phase: Thermal and Nonthermal Emission, Magnetic Topology, and Flux Rope Confinement
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures; published in The Astrophysical Journal (2026)
summary: We study a long-duration, confined X2.0-class solar flare exhibiting three distinct episodes of HXR emission, along with an accompanying EUV late phase. A key highlight of this work is the novel observations from the high-resolution solar X-ray spectrometers SoLEXS and HEL1OS onboard Aditya-L1, providing insights into the evolution of thermal and non-thermal emissions. Simultaneous EUV observations from AIA/SDO in hot channels, combined with multi-band X-ray light curves, reveal a two-stage confined eruption of a large MFR, separated by $\sim$10~minutes. The first stage corresponds to an M4.6 flare, while the overall event reaches X2.0 on the GOES scale. During the first phase, magnetic reconnection beneath the large EUV hot channel causes plasma heating to $\sim$19~MK, with a non-thermal spectral index of $\sim$4.3. In the second phase, characterized by external reconnection and confinement of the MFR hot channel, the temperature increases to $\sim$22~MK, accompanied by further hardening of the spectral index to $\sim$3.9. Despite pronounced non-thermal signatures and enhanced particle acceleration, the MFR fails to erupt through the overlying coronal loops because of the strong strapping force exerted by the large overlying coronal loops. Importantly, the stalled eruption, together with reconnection in the higher overlying loops, results in enhanced heating within a closed magnetic configuration, with temperatures peaking at up to $\sim$15~MK during the late phase. The paper also provides the first observations of detectable non-thermal X-ray emission during the early EUV late phase, albeit briefly, providing direct evidence for reconnection-induced heating, likely occurring in the higher overlying coronal loops.

AI.tldr: A confined X2.0 solar flare with a two-stage magnetic flux rope eruption and EUV late phase is analyzed using novel Aditya-L1 X-ray spectra, revealing thermal/non-thermal evolution, spectral hardening, and reconnection-driven late-phase heating with the first detection of non-thermal X-ray emission in the early EUV late phase.
AI.motivation: To understand the evolution of thermal and non-thermal emissions during a long-duration confined flare, particularly the mechanisms driving multi-episode HXR emission and the EUV late phase.
AI.method: Analysis of a confined X2.0 flare using high-resolution solar X-ray spectrometers SoLEXS and HEL1OS onboard Aditya-L1, combined with EUV observations from AIA/SDO hot channels and multi-band X-ray light curves to diagnose thermal and non-thermal emission and magnetic reconnection.
AI.result: A two-stage confined eruption of a large MFR separated by ~10 minutes (first stage M4.6, overall X2.0). Phase 1: reconnection beneath the hot channel heats plasma to ~19 MK with non-thermal spectral index ~4.3. Phase 2: external reconnection and MFR confinement raises temperature to ~22 MK and hardens the spectral index to ~3.9. The MFR stalls due to strong strapping force from overlying loops; the stalled eruption and higher-loop reconnection cause late-phase heating up to ~15 MK. First detection of non-thermal X-ray emission during the early EUV late phase was achieved.
AI.conclusion: The confined X2.0 flare is driven by a two-stage MFR eruption, with progression from phase 1 to phase 2 marked by increased temperature and spectral hardening. Strong strapping force from overlying coronal loops prevents the MFR from erupting, and the resulting stalled eruption and higher-loop reconnection power the EUV late-phase heating, offering direct evidence of reconnection-induced heating.

title: An Intermediate-orbit Brown Dwarf Confirmed with Astrometry+Radial Velocity Joint Analysis, and the Eccentricity Distribution of Brown Dwarfs Across Different Locations
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables, accepted for publication in AJ
summary: Intermediate-orbit ($\sim 1$ AU) brown dwarfs with absolute mass measurements are essential for understanding the evolution of substellar objects. Although such systems remain rare, their number is now being enlarged thanks to astrometry. Here, we present the absolute mass measurements for HD 203771B, a massive brown dwarf orbiting a K dwarf ($M_\ast=0.79\pm0.08\ M_\odot$) with a period of 1140 days on an eccentric ($e\approx0.5$) and inclined ($i\approx 130^{\circ}$) orbit. Through joint analysis of (1) radial velocities and Gaia two-body solution, as well as (2) radial velocities, Hipparcos Intermediate Astrometric Data and two-epoch Gaia astrometry, we obtain true companion masses of $74.20^{+3.46}_{-3.64} M_{\mathrm{J}}$ and $69.03^{+4.99}_{-4.95} M_{\mathrm{J}}$, respectively, agreeing with each other within $1σ$. Taking a sample of 159 brown dwarfs with absolute mass measurements from different detection techniques, we investigate their eccentricity distributions across different semi-major axis ranges by fitting a Beta distribution. We find that the peak of eccentricity distribution tends to gradually shift toward lower values from wide orbits ($a>20$ AU) to intermediate ($1<a<20$ AU) and inner ($0.1<a<1$ AU) regions. Such trend is plausibly due to disk friction during orbital evolution. Together with obliquity studies showing that brown dwarfs are mostly aligned, our result suggests that brown dwarfs may migrate inward through quiescent coplanar disk-driven processes.

AI.tldr: The paper reports absolute mass measurements for the intermediate-orbit brown dwarf HD 203771B and, from a sample of 159 brown dwarfs, finds that the eccentricity distribution peak shifts to lower values from wide to inner orbits, suggesting quiescent coplanar disk-driven inward migration.
AI.motivation: Intermediate-orbit (~1 AU) brown dwarfs with absolute mass measurements are essential for understanding substellar evolution, yet such systems remain rare. Astrometry is now enlarging this sample, and the eccentricity distributions of brown dwarfs across semi-major axis ranges, plus their migration pathways, remain poorly constrained.
AI.method: The authors measure the absolute mass of HD 203771B, a massive brown dwarf orbiting a K dwarf (M*=0.79±0.08 Msun, P=1140 days, e≈0.5, i≈130°), via two joint analyses: (1) radial velocities plus the Gaia two-body solution, and (2) radial velocities, Hipparcos Intermediate Astrometric Data, and two-epoch Gaia astrometry. They then compile 159 brown dwarfs with absolute mass measurements from various detection techniques and fit a Beta distribution to their eccentricity distributions across different semi-major axis ranges.
AI.result: The two independent analyses yield true companion masses of 74.20+3.46-3.64 MJ and 69.03+4.99-4.95 MJ, agreeing within 1σ. For the 159-brown-dwarf sample, the peak of the eccentricity distribution gradually shifts toward lower values from wide orbits (a>20 AU) to intermediate (1<a<20 AU) and inner (0.1<a<1 AU) regions.
AI.conclusion: The observed eccentricity trend with orbital separation is plausibly caused by disk friction during orbital evolution. Combined with obliquity studies showing brown dwarfs are mostly aligned, this suggests that brown dwarfs may migrate inward through quiescent, coplanar, disk-driven processes.

title: TESS flares and chromospheric variability in the Pleiades, the Hyades, and Praesepe
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Magnetic activity is a result of the interaction between rotation and dynamo processes in cool stars with outer convection zones. Since open cluster members share a common age, distance, and chemical composition, they provide an opportunity to study the magnetic activity of cool stars in a controlled astrophysical context. We used 120s cadence observations from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) to study the flare activity of stars in three open clusters with different ages: the Pleiades (100 Myr), the Hyades (700 Myr) and Praesepe (700 Myr). We used the Ohio State Multi-Object Spectrograph (OSMOS) at MDM Observatory with the goal of identifying coronal mass ejections (CMEs) in the Pleiades and Praesepe. We investigated the flaring characteristics of the cluster members using the TESS light curves: we identified the flares, then divided the dataset into different categories based on the effective temperature and light curve amplitude. We calculated the flare energies and investigated the flare frequency distributions. We studied the dynamic spectra of the H$α$ line and its environment to search for indication of CMEs. The power-law indices of the flare frequency distributions obtained in our analysis span the 1.8-2.8 range. We found the highest flare rates in the Pleiades for all investigated spectral types. Our results show that the flare rate of M dwarfs is similar in the Pleiades and the Hyades while for K-type stars the flare rate in the Pleiades is an order of magnitude higher. Our analysis reveals that the flare rate in M stars changes with their effective temperature: the rate is highest for T$_{eff}$ $\sim$3200-3300 K -coinciding with the transition between partially and fully convective stars - with smooth decrease in flare rate towards cooler and hotter M dwarfs. We used the MDM/OSMOS spectra to place an upper limit on the CME rate.

AI.tldr: TESS 120s-cadence photometry of Pleiades, Hyades, and Praesepe members reveals flare frequency distribution power-law indices of 1.8–2.8, the highest flare rates in the Pleiades, and an M-dwarf flare-rate peak near T_eff ~3200–3300 K, with MDM/OSMOS spectra used to constrain the CME rate.
AI.motivation: Magnetic activity arises from the interplay of rotation and dynamo action in cool stars with outer convection zones. Open clusters are ideal laboratories because their members share age, distance, and chemical composition, enabling a controlled study of how magnetic activity evolves with age and stellar parameters.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 120s-cadence TESS light curves of stars in three open clusters of different ages—Pleiades (100 Myr), Hyades (700 Myr), and Praesepe (700 Myr). They identified flares, categorized the dataset by effective temperature and light-curve amplitude, computed flare energies, and derived flare frequency distributions. Additionally, they obtained MDM Observatory OSMOS spectra of the Pleiades and Praesepe, examining Hα dynamic spectra and their surroundings to search for CME signatures.
AI.result: The flare frequency distributions yielded power-law indices spanning 1.8–2.8. The Pleiades showed the highest flare rates across all investigated spectral types. M-dwarf flare rates were similar in the Pleiades and Hyades, whereas K-type flare rates were an order of magnitude higher in the Pleiades. Among M stars, flare rate peaked at T_eff ~3200–3300 K—coinciding with the transition between partially and fully convective stars—and decreased smoothly toward both cooler and hotter M dwarfs.
AI.conclusion: Flare activity in cool cluster stars depends strongly on age and spectral type, with the Pleiades generally showing enhanced flaring relative to the older clusters. The M-dwarf flare-rate maximum near the partial-to-fully convective transition points to a dynamo-related dependence on internal structure. The MDM/OSMOS spectra provided only an upper limit on the CME rate.

title: The nearby Type II supernova 2024ggi beyond 600 days: circumstellar interaction and dust formation
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures; submitted for publication in A&A
summary: The Type II SN 2024ggi is one of the nearest core-collapse SNe to have exploded in recent decades. Its proximity has enabled extensive multiwavelength monitoring from early times through the nebular phase. Signatures of late-time interaction between the SN ejecta and hydrogen-rich circumstellar material (CSM) have recently been reported. Here we extend its study using late-time optical photometry and spectroscopy from 570 to 820 d after explosion. We investigate the emergence and evolution of late-time ejecta-CSM interaction and constrain the geometry of the interaction region and the properties of newly formed dust. Comparisons with other interacting SNe II and with synthetic spectra are presented. We model the H$α$ profile with the Monte Carlo radiative-transfer code Damocles, including both gas and dust components. Spectroscopic signatures of interaction precede the photometric flattening. The spectra evolve from ejecta-dominated to interaction-dominated as H$α$ develops a broad, boxy profile. The optical light curves subsequently flatten relative to the $^{56}$Co decay rate at approximately 650-670 d. The emission lines show a systematic blue-to-red asymmetry that requires a dust component newly formed within the ejecta. The inferred dust mass formed in the ejecta is $10^{-6}-10^{-5}$ M$_\odot$ if the grains are amorphous carbon or a carbon-silicate mixture, but can reach up to $10^{-3}$ M$_\odot$ for pure silicates.

AI.tldr: Late-time optical photometry and spectroscopy of SN 2024ggi reveal the emergence of ejecta-CSM interaction and newly formed dust, with interaction signatures preceding photometric flattening.
AI.motivation: SN 2024ggi is one of the nearest core-collapse SNe in recent decades, enabling extensive multiwavelength monitoring. Recent reports of late-time ejecta-CSM interaction motivate an extended study of its late-time evolution and dust formation.
AI.method: Late-time optical photometry and spectroscopy from 570 to 820 d after explosion. The H-alpha profile is modeled with the Monte Carlo radiative-transfer code Damocles, including gas and dust components. Comparisons are made with other interacting SNe II and synthetic spectra.
AI.result: Spectroscopic interaction signatures precede the photometric flattening. Spectra evolve from ejecta-dominated to interaction-dominated, with H-alpha developing a broad, boxy profile. Light curves flatten relative to the Co-56 decay rate at ~650-670 d. Emission lines show blue-to-red asymmetry requiring newly formed ejecta dust. Inferred dust mass is 1e-6 to 1e-5 solar masses for amorphous carbon or carbon-silicate mixtures, up to 1e-3 solar masses for pure silicates.
AI.conclusion: Late-time ejecta-CSM interaction and newly formed dust govern the nebular-phase evolution of SN 2024ggi, with dust composition strongly affecting the inferred dust mass.

title: From Giant Envelopes to Rapidly Contracting Cores in Rotating Population III Stars from $500$ to $1000 \, M_\odot$
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome
summary: Population III (Pop III) stars link the chemical enrichment of the early Universe to the formation of the first massive black holes, yet their evolution remains poorly understood at extreme masses. Using GENEC, we evolve rotating zero metallicity models from $500$ to $1000\,M_\odot$ at $v/v_{\rm crit}=0.1$ through core Si burning, and a $1000\,M_\odot$, $v/v_{\rm crit}=0.4$ model evolved through He exhaustion. In the fiducial $1000\,M_\odot$ model, convection and rotational transport carry freshly synthesized C and O into H burning layers, producing $62.1\,M_\odot$ of primary N by He exhaustion. Surface mass loss removes $20.2\,M_\odot$, including $1.8\times10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ of N, with $\log(\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{O})=0.68$, $\log(\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{C})=1.48$, and $\log(\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{O})=-0.80$. By the final hydrostatic model, the inner $100\,M_\odot$ is confined within $0.088\,R_\odot$ while the photosphere remains several thousand solar radii away. As C, Ne, O, and Si burning accelerate, chemical mixing freezes out and advanced products remain buried beneath the envelope. At core Si exhaustion, the central angular velocity reaches $4\times10^{-3}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$ while the surface rotates at $5.25\times10^{-8}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$, a contrast of $7.6\times10^4$. Contraction drives this spin up, while inner specific angular momentum changes by less than $1\%$. The maximum $j_{\rm eq}/j_{\rm ISCO}$ is $0.313$, limiting disk formation in our inside out estimate. These models show that Pop~III stars can produce strong primary N signatures and rapidly rotating black hole progenitors while their envelopes determine which products enrich the early Universe.

AI.tldr: Rotating zero-metallicity GENEC models of 500–1000 M⊙ Pop III stars show efficient primary N production and extreme internal angular-momentum stratification, shaping black hole progenitor evolution.
AI.motivation: Pop III stars connect early-Universe chemical enrichment to the formation of the first massive black holes, but their evolution at extreme masses remains poorly understood.
AI.method: Rotating, zero-metallicity GENEC stellar evolution models from 500 to 1000 M⊙ at v/v_crit = 0.1, evolved through core Si burning; a 1000 M⊙, v/v_crit = 0.4 model evolved through He exhaustion.
AI.result: Fiducial 1000 M⊙ model yields 62.1 M⊙ of primary N by He exhaustion; surface mass loss removes 20.2 M⊙ (including 1.8×10⁻³ M⊙ N) with log(N/O)=0.68, log(N/C)=1.48, log(C/O)=-0.80. Inner 100 M⊙ confined within 0.088 R⊙; chemical mixing freezes out during advanced burning. At core Si exhaustion, central angular velocity 4×10⁻³ s⁻¹ vs. surface 5.25×10⁻⁸ s⁻¹ (contrast 7.6×10⁴), with inner specific angular momentum changing <1%. Maximum j_eq/j_ISCO = 0.313, limiting disk formation.
AI.conclusion: Pop III stars can produce strong primary N signatures and rapidly rotating black hole progenitors, while their envelopes dictate which products enrich the early Universe.

title: An upper limit on Galactic OB+black hole binaries from SDSS-V
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Binaries composed of a luminous OB star and a black hole (BH) are a key evolutionary link between massive stellar binaries and merging compact-object binaries, but only a handful are known and their occurrence fraction remains poorly constrained. We use multi-epoch spectroscopy from the SDSS-V Milky Way Mapper to place a first rigorous empirical upper limit on the fraction of Galactic massive ($\geq 10\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) OB stars with a close BH companion, $f_\mathrm{BH}$. Radial-velocity (RV) variability alone cannot distinguish BH companions from the far more numerous luminous binaries. We therefore combine the SDSS-V RV variability measurements of 3130 massive OB stars with high-resolution follow-up and literature information to identify luminous companions among the RV-variable subset. Forward-modelling the detectability of OB+BH systems using BH masses and orbital parameters from binary-evolution models, we find $f_\mathrm{BH} \lesssim 3\%$ at 95% credibility. This empirical upper limit approaches, but does not exclude, theoretical predictions for the OB+BH fraction. The constraint is primarily limited by the number of RV-variable systems that can be decisively classified, highlighting the importance of complete, high-quality follow-up for future searches.

AI.tldr: Using SDSS-V multi-epoch spectroscopy of 3130 massive OB stars plus follow-up, the authors derive a first rigorous 95% credibility upper limit on the Galactic OB+BH close-binary fraction: f_BH ≲ 3%.
AI.motivation: OB+BH binaries link massive stellar binaries to merging compact-object binaries, but only a few are known and their occurrence fraction is poorly constrained. An empirical upper limit is needed to test binary-evolution predictions.
AI.method: Combine SDSS-V Milky Way Mapper radial-velocity variability measurements of 3130 massive (≥10 M_sun) OB stars with high-resolution follow-up and literature data to identify luminous companions among RV variables. Forward-model OB+BH detectability using BH masses and orbital parameters from binary-evolution models.
AI.result: f_BH ≲ 3% at 95% credibility. The limit approaches, but does not exclude, theoretical predictions for the OB+BH fraction.
AI.conclusion: The constraint is primarily limited by the number of RV-variable systems that can be decisively classified, highlighting the importance of complete, high-quality follow-up for future searches.

title: Henrietta Leavitt's classical Cepheid relation
comment: submitted
summary: The Leavitt & Pickering (1912) mean period-magnitude relation for SMC Cepheids exhibits correlated residuals relative to modern Gaia $B_G$ and Johnson $V$ photometry ($r_{δV/δL12}\approx0.76$). Therefore dispersion inherent to Leavitt's photographic photometry relation is not solely random scatter ($σ_{L12,B_G,V}=0.22\pm0.03,0.25\pm0.04,0.20\pm0^{m}.03$), and is potentially consistent with the partial encoding of combined effects from the elongated SMC, classical Cepheid instability strip, differential reddening, etc. OGLE data indicate that $\gtrsim870$ SMC variables identified by Leavitt (1908, Table 2) are classical Cepheids ($\gtrsim 90$ %), and the preliminary unphased Table 2 photometry likewise features correlated residuals relative to contemporary observations ($r_{δB_G/δL08-T2}\approx0.54$). Table 6 data in Leavitt (1908, $n=16$) define a highly linear Leavitt law over an extensive baseline ($r\approx-0.98$), but constitute a smaller sample than the later 1912 work ($n=25$).

AI.tldr: Leavitt's historical period-magnitude relations for SMC Cepheids show correlated (not purely random) residuals versus modern Gaia/Johnson photometry, consistent with partial encoding of structural and reddening effects; OGLE data confirm most Leavitt (1908) variables are classical Cepheids.
AI.motivation: To assess whether the dispersion in Leavitt's original photographic period-magnitude relations reflects solely random scatter or instead encodes systematic physical effects, using modern photometry as a benchmark.
AI.method: Compare residuals of the Leavitt & Pickering (1912) mean period-magnitude relation (n=25) against modern Gaia B_G and Johnson V photometry via correlation analysis; similarly analyze the unphased Leavitt (1908) Table 2 photometry; classify the 1908 variables with OGLE data; and model the Leavitt (1908) Table 6 relation (n=16).
AI.result: The 1912 relation residuals are correlated (r=0.76) with modern photometry, with dispersions σ=0.22±0.03 (B_G), 0.25±0.04 (V), 0.20±0.03 mag. OGLE confirms ≳870 (≳90%) of Leavitt's Table 2 variables are classical Cepheids, and their residuals also correlate (r=0.54). The 1908 Table 6 relation is highly linear (r≈−0.98) over a large baseline but uses a smaller sample than 1912.
AI.conclusion: The scatter in Leavitt's photographic relations is not purely random but partly reflects combined effects such as the elongated SMC geometry, the instability strip, and differential reddening, validating the enduring value of her Cepheid samples.

title: What Does 2D Coronal Seismology Measure?
comment: 29 pages, 14 figures, accepted by ApJ
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) coronal seismology based on coronagraphic imaging spectroscopy has emerged as a promising method for mapping the coronal magnetic field, but the physical meaning of its inferred quantities under optically thin line-of-sight (LOS) integration remains uncertain. We investigate this problem by synthesizing coronagraphic observables from a global wave-driven magnetohydrodynamic model with a long LOS extent and a structured corona, and by applying the same analysis procedures used for observations. We compare the diagnosed density, wave propagation direction, phase speed, and magnetic-field strength with different LOS-weighted reference quantities from the model. We find that the measured density and the wave propagation direction are both well represented by LOS emissivity-weighted quantities. In contrast, the phase speed is not controlled by emissivity weighting alone: the LOS distribution of wave velocity amplitude also plays an important role. As a result, the inferred magnetic field is better represented by combining the emissivity-weighted density with an amplitude-dependent effective speed. Emissivity weighting nevertheless remains a reasonable approximation, and a useful baseline, over much of the field of view, especially where the LOS does not cross strongly structured plasma-sheet-like regions. These results clarify the physical interpretation of 2D coronal seismology and provide guidance for future coronal magnetic-field tomography and model-constrained applications.

AI.motivation: 2D coronal seismology from coronagraphic imaging spectroscopy is a promising way to map the coronal magnetic field, yet it is unclear what the inferred quantities physically mean under optically thin line-of-sight (LOS) integration.

title: A breath of fresh air: Oxygen enhancement from silicate sublimation during early protostellar evolution
comment: Accepted to A&A, 9 pages, 4 figures, 1 table
summary: Recently, an analog to the t = 0 moment of our Solar System's meteoritic record was identified for the first time around the Class I protostar HOPS-315. Crystalline silicates were found to recondense from SiO gas that cools as it advects upward from a hot thermostat region in the inner midplane. This t=0 moment may be associated with the formation of the first planetesimals in this disk. We explore whether HOPS-68, a Class I protostar with similar properties and system geometries, is engaged in such refractory recondensation as well. A detection of cooler gas-phase SiO in absorption above a hot disk midplane would allow us to achieve this goal, thanks to a previous detection of crystalline silicates. HOPS-68 was observed with the JWST MIRI and NIRSpec, showing multiple bands of molecular absorption. We use local thermal equilibrium slab models to measure the temperature, column density, velocity, and radial location of these bands. The molecular absorption bands of gaseous SiO, H2O, CO2, and 13CO trace a warm molecular inversion layer (300-500 K) at mid-altitudes above the hot disk midplane from 0.3-16 AU, which is consistently blue-shifted with respect to the system velocity by 33-53 km/s. Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations of HOPS-68 kinematically resolve an SiO-rich jet and wind. We confirm that HOPS-68, like HOPS-315, is undergoing an epoch analogous to the t=0 moment in the Solar System's planet formation timeline. The detected warm molecular layer traces the base of a disk wind, which carries sublimated material from the thermostat region near 2 AU up into the outer disk. As for HOPS-315, the molecular layer in the inner few AU of HOPS-68 is enhanced in bulk oxygen as a result of this sublimation. Since HOPS-68 is less evolved than HOPS-315, this may indicate a prolonged epoch in protostellar evolution in which such oxygen enhancement occurs.

AI.motivation: A t=0 analog was recently identified around HOPS-315, where crystalline silicates recondense from cooling SiO gas advecting upward from a hot thermostat region. The authors test whether HOPS-68, a Class I protostar with similar properties and geometry, undergoes the same refractory recondensation.
AI.method: HOPS-68 was observed with JWST MIRI and NIRSpec, revealing multiple molecular absorption bands. Local thermal equilibrium slab models were used to derive temperature, column density, velocity, and radial location. Complementary ALMA observations kinematically resolved an SiO-rich jet and wind.

AI.conclusion: HOPS-68, like HOPS-315, is undergoing an epoch analogous to the Solar System's t=0 planet formation moment. The warm molecular layer traces the base of a disk wind carrying sublimated material from the ~2 AU thermostat region into the outer disk, yielding bulk oxygen enhancement in the inner few AU. As HOPS-68 is less evolved than HOPS-315, this suggests a prolonged evolutionary epoch during which such oxygen enhancement occurs.

title: Revisiting the Role of Global Magnetic Variables in Coronal Heating of Solar Active RegionsDavid H. Brooks
comment: To be published in The Astrophysical Journal. The machine readable table referenced in the text will be available in the journal version. The abstract is abridged for arXiv
summary: Reconnection-based models of coronal heating predict that magnetic complexity---non-potential configurations, currents, shear---should enhance coronal emission independently of total magnetic flux. Previous work, however, found no evidence that complexity contributes independently to coronal heating (Fisher et al. 1998). We revisit this question using SDO/HMI vector magnetograms and SDO/AIA EUV imaging. HMI Space-weather Active Region Patches (SHARPs) provide 16 magnetic parameters characterizing field strength, gradients, currents, helicity, and non-potentiality. We measure spatially-integrated transition region and coronal emission using AIA 304A, 193A, 94A, and isolated Fe XVIII emission for 137 active regions, sampling plasma at ~0.09MK, ~1.4MK, and ~7.1MK. Partial correlation analysis isolates the contribution of each complexity parameter after controlling for total unsigned vertical magnetic flux. Unsigned flux (Phi_M) explains 72--82\% of variance in emission, following power laws (I ~ Phi_M^alpha, where alpha=0.61-1.19) consistent with prior soft X-ray results. Partial correlations reveal weak positive contributions (r = 0.2-0.3) to transition region (304A) emission from some vertical current and field parameters, but little evidence that other active-region-averaged measures of magnetic complexity enhance coronal emission. The exception is total photospheric magnetic free energy density (rho_tot), which shows a positive partial correlation (r = 0.49, p < 0.001) with Fe XVIII emission, but negative, or non-existent, partial correlations with other AIA filters. These results suggest quasi-steady coronal heating scales with magnetic flux, while rho_tot may contribute to high temperature coronal heating. At lower temperatures, regions with more stored energy than expected for their flux produce less EUV emission than expected.

Using SDO/HMI SHARPs and SDO/AIA EUV imaging for 137 active regions, the authors apply partial correlation analysis to isolate complexity contributions beyond unsigned flux. Flux explains 72–82% of emission variance (I ~ Phi_M^alpha, alpha=0.61–1.19), while most complexity parameters show only weak or negligible independent contributions, except free energy density (rho_tot), which correlates positively with high-temperature Fe XVIII emission but negatively with cooler filters.
AI.motivation: Reconnection-based coronal heating models predict that magnetic complexity (non-potential configurations, currents, shear) should enhance coronal emission independently of total magnetic flux, yet earlier work (Fisher et al. 1998) found no such independent contribution. This study revisits the question with modern vector magnetograms and multi-wavelength EUV imaging to test whether any complexity measures contribute beyond unsigned flux.

Spatially-integrated transition region and coronal emission is measured with SDO/AIA 304A, 193A, 94A, and isolated Fe XVIII emission, sampling plasma at ~0.09 MK, ~1.4 MK, and ~7.1 MK. Partial correlation analysis isolates each complexity parameter's contribution after controlling for total unsigned vertical magnetic flux.

Partial correlations show weak positive contributions (r = 0.2–0.3) to transition region (304A) emission from some vertical current and field parameters, but little evidence that other active-region-averaged complexity measures enhance coronal emission.
